rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to capture all 10 compounds and reveal the retention range and critical separations. A moderate gradient duration leaves ample final-strength hold for strongly retained compounds.

Halve the gradient duration to reduce the time penalty while testing whether the current resolution margin survives compression. Keep temperature and endpoints fixed to isolate the gradient-slope effect.

Use a slightly shallower gradient to improve the compressed central separations, while raising temperature to test selectivity changes and offset the extra retention time. The target is full resolution with the last peak still in the zero-time-penalty region.

Test a 5 °C temperature increase for a faster alternative that might retain the maximum CRF. Keeping the gradient unchanged isolates temperature-dependent selectivity, particularly for the two pairs near the resolution threshold.

Return to the successful 55 °C selectivity and raise the starting organic fraction slightly to test an alternative maximum-score method. The slightly shallower gradient may improve the marginal central separation while the stronger start reduces retention.

Preserve injection 3’s initial composition, temperature, and gradient slope of 0.075 organic fraction per minute using a lower endpoint and shorter gradient. All peaks previously eluted before this gradient would end, so this distinct program should retain the maximum CRF.

Keep the proven gradient slope and temperature while lowering the endpoint to 0.65. The gradient still extends beyond the last observed peak, so this program should preserve CRF 1.000 with a lower final organic fraction.

Test a shallower gradient at 50 °C to seek a larger resolution margin than the current maximum-score method. Lower temperature should improve the temperature-sensitive central separation, while the shallower slope may compensate for compression of the other critical pair.

Return to 55 °C and test a small decrease in gradient slope relative to injection 3. This probes whether the two marginal central separations can be better balanced while retaining the maximum CRF and zero time penalty.

Combine the higher starting organic fraction, which improved the later critical pair in injection 5, with a shallower gradient to recover resolution of the earlier critical pair. This tests an alternative maximum-score method with potentially better separation margins and no time penalty.

Extend the successful combination of a stronger start and shallower gradient to seek greater resolution margins while maintaining CRF 1.000. Monitor the early peaks for compression as well as the two critical central separations.

Use a slightly shallower gradient than injection 10 at the same starting composition and temperature to improve the earlier critical separation. The later critical pair should remain near its successful resolution range, with the last peak expected around 8.6 minutes.

Slightly flatten injection 11’s gradient to recover its under-resolved central pair while preserving the stronger separation of the later critical pair. This may provide another maximum-score method with a more balanced resolution margin and no time penalty.

Reduce the gradient slope modestly from injection 13 to raise its limiting resolution above 1.5 while retaining the later pair’s margin. The last peak is projected near 9 minutes, testing whether full resolution is achievable before a time penalty appears.

Increase the gradient slope slightly relative to injection 10 to shorten retention while keeping its limiting resolution above 1.5. This targets a faster maximum-score alternative with a balanced margin between the two critical central pairs.

With the maximum CRF already secured, test a distinctly lower-temperature selectivity regime using the fast scouting gradient. Temperature-driven changes in elution order may resolve the central cluster and reveal an alternative maximum-score method.
Return to the successful 55 °C region with a gradient slope between injections 10 and 12. This should preserve full resolution and zero time penalty, providing another maximum-score option.

Preserve injection 10’s starting composition, temperature, and gradient slope while reducing the endpoint and gradient duration. Because its last peak eluted before this program’s gradient reaches the outlet endpoint at 8.65 minutes, the separation should retain CRF 1.000.

Keep the proven initial composition, temperature, and slope but end the gradient earlier to test a lower-organic hold. The critical central separations should remain unchanged; the main question is whether the last compound still elutes without a time penalty.

Test a gradient slope between the successful injections 12 and 17, keeping starting composition and temperature fixed. This should maintain full resolution and zero time penalty, further defining the maximum-score operating range.

Test a lower endpoint with a slope close to injection 12’s successful gradient. The central separations should remain resolved; this checks whether the final hold still brings the last peak out within the zero-time-penalty window.

Use a gradient slope bracketed by successful injections 17 and 20, with an endpoint reached after all peaks should elute. This is expected to preserve CRF 1.000 while providing a shorter programmed gradient than those two methods.

Extend the successful gradient-slope range slightly below injection 21 while keeping the endpoint high enough to avoid a hold-related delay. The observed trends suggest full resolution and a last peak just under 9 minutes, potentially retaining CRF 1.000.

Test a slope just below injection 9’s successful gradient to refine the maximum-score boundary at the lower starting composition. The earlier critical pair should improve, while the later pair will determine whether full resolution is retained.

With the maximum CRF already secured, use the final injection to test a slightly faster gradient than injection 15. This probes the fast edge of the maximum-score region, with the earlier central pair most likely to limit resolution.
